Pregnancy

Buttock pain during pregnancy: finding the cause and relief

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

An unexpected pain in your bottom can make sitting, walking or resting difficult during pregnancy. Different causes need different care. The most useful first step is to describe the pattern and check for warning symptoms, then make a treatment plan with your maternity team.

Start with the location and pattern of the pain

Pain described as being in the bottom can arise from several places. Soreness at the anus during a bowel movement is different from a deep ache at the back of the pelvis or an electric pain travelling down a leg. Pregnancy can make these problems more likely or more uncomfortable, but the location alone does not identify the cause.

Notice when the pain began, which side is affected, what brings it on and whether it reaches the back, groin or leg. Tell your maternity team how it affects walking, sleep, sitting and using the toilet. You do not need to wait until pain becomes unbearable to ask for an assessment.

Pelvic girdle pain can spread into the buttocks

Pelvic girdle pain involves the joints and surrounding structures at the front or back of the pelvis. It affects about one in five pregnant people. A growing bump, altered posture and changes in how the pelvis bears weight may contribute; this is not simply proof that the baby is too heavy.

Symptoms can include aching around the buttocks, hips or groin, clicking or grinding, and pain when walking, using stairs or turning in bed. A physiotherapist familiar with pregnancy can help distinguish this from other causes. Confirmed pelvic girdle pain itself does not harm the baby and usually does not prevent a vaginal birth. Pain in this area does not predict the baby’s sex.

Sciatica usually includes symptoms down a leg

The sciatic nerve runs from the lower back through the buttock and down the leg. When it is irritated or compressed, pain may feel burning, shooting or electric. Tingling, numbness or weakness may accompany pain extending toward the foot. An ache confined to the buttock is not enough to diagnose sciatica.

Pregnancy-related changes can contribute to back and nerve symptoms, but do not assume that a change in the baby’s position means the baby is sitting directly on the nerve. Several back problems can produce a similar pattern. Assessment is particularly useful when pain worsens, persists or limits ordinary activity; new neurological warning symptoms need emergency care.

Haemorrhoids cause pain around the anus

Haemorrhoids, also called piles, are swollen vascular cushions inside or around the anus. Pregnancy can increase pressure in this area, and constipation or straining can worsen symptoms. You may notice itching, soreness, a lump or bright red blood after passing stool. Long periods sitting or standing can add discomfort.

A fissure, a clot in an external haemorrhoid or an infection can also cause pain. Do not assume that significant bleeding, fever or a rapidly worsening painful lump is an ordinary pile. Tell a clinician about new or persistent rectal bleeding so that the cause can be checked rather than repeatedly treating it yourself.

Contractions can be felt in the back and bottom

Labour discomfort is not identical for everyone. Tightening in the abdomen may come with backache, pelvic pressure or pain felt toward the bottom. Labour contractions tend to become stronger, longer and more regular. Braxton Hicks tightenings are usually irregular and do not progressively build in the same way, but the distinction is not always obvious at home.

Contact your maternity service if you think labour is starting or are unsure about painful tightenings. Seek urgent advice for possible labour before 37 weeks, vaginal bleeding, a change in your baby’s usual movements or suspected leaking waters. Waters may come as a small continuing trickle as well as a gush; do not wait for a dramatic release of fluid.

Know when pain needs urgent or emergency assessment

Get emergency care for new numbness around the genitals or anus, difficulty starting or passing urine, loss of bladder or bowel control, or severe or worsening weakness or numbness affecting both legs with back or leg pain. These can indicate serious compression of the nerves at the base of the spine. Do not wait to see whether a pillow or painkiller helps.

Severe constant pain, fever, feeling very unwell, or an anal swelling with spreading redness also needs prompt assessment. Heavy or continuous rectal bleeding, large clots or faintness requires urgent medical help. If you are unsure whether blood or fluid is coming from the vagina or the anus, explain that uncertainty when calling rather than assuming it is harmless.

Adapt movement and rest to the cause

For pelvic girdle pain, try sitting to dress, spreading weight evenly through both feet and reducing repeated heavy lifting or one-legged tasks. Keeping the knees comfortably together while turning in bed or getting out of a car can help some people; do not force a painful movement. Use a pillow between the legs and, if useful, beneath the bump when resting on your side.

Change position regularly and balance manageable activity with rest. A fitted pelvic support belt or another aid may help after assessment. Sciatica may need a different exercise plan, so avoid copying aggressive stretches or using a belt as a cure for every cause. Ask for help with chores that provoke pain. If you become very immobile, your maternity team should review both treatment and blood-clot risk.

Use simple comfort measures without ignoring the cause

A comfortably warm bath or shower may ease tense muscles. For local soreness, a wrapped cool or warm pack can be tried briefly if your care team agrees; protect the skin and avoid excessive heat. A warm sitz bath lets the anal area rest in shallow water and may soothe haemorrhoid discomfort. It is a comfort measure, not a treatment for an abscess or heavy bleeding.

For piles, keep stools easier to pass with fibre from fruit, vegetables and whole grains, enough fluid and suitable activity. Avoid straining and lingering on the toilet. Gentle cleaning and patting dry can reduce irritation. Check haemorrhoid creams, suppositories and stool-softening medicines with a pharmacist or maternity clinician so that the product and duration suit pregnancy.

Choose medicines for your pregnancy and your symptoms

Paracetamol, also called acetaminophen, can be used during pregnancy when appropriate and taken as directed. Check the dose, duration and other products you use so that you do not accidentally duplicate it. It may help some painful conditions but is not a reliable treatment for every kind of nerve pain. Repeated or worsening pain needs a diagnosis as well as symptom relief.

Ibuprofen and other NSAIDs are not interchangeable pregnancy options. Avoid self-treating with them from around 20 weeks onward unless a clinician specifically advises it; later pregnancy brings additional risks. Prescribed low-dose aspirin has a different purpose and should not be stopped because of a general painkiller warning.

Severe pain may sometimes justify a stronger prescription medicine, including an opioid such as oxycodone or hydrocodone, after an individual assessment. These are not a routine next step or a standard one-week course for buttock pain. Do not borrow medicines or abruptly stop established treatment. The aim is appropriate treatment with understood benefits and risks, rather than leaving important pain untreated to avoid every medicine.

Keep a follow-up plan after birth

Many pregnancy-related pelvic symptoms improve after birth, but recovery varies and pain is not guaranteed to disappear immediately. Haemorrhoids can also persist or first become troublesome after delivery. Continue the agreed care plan and arrange reassessment if symptoms are not improving or interfere with caring for yourself or the baby.

Ask what improvement to expect, when to return and which symptoms should prompt an earlier call. A diagnosis made during pregnancy should not prevent a fresh assessment of a new or different pain after birth. Physiotherapy, constipation treatment and other care can be adjusted as your recovery progresses.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Pelvic girdle pain, radiating nerve pain and anal pain should be assessed as different patterns.

Pregnancy-specific medicine advice takes priority over general back-pain recommendations.

How BeMama can help

Record where the pain is and what triggers it, and ask for practical help before daily tasks become unmanageable.

When to seek help

New saddle numbness or bladder/bowel dysfunction needs emergency assessment. Contact maternity care urgently for leaking waters, bleeding, reduced movements or possible preterm labour.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • You do not have to wait until birth to seek help.
  • Keeping knees comfortably together can help pelvic girdle movements; avoid forcing painful positions.
  • Heavy bleeding, neurological changes and maternity warning signs need prompt care.
  • Medicines and follow-up should fit the diagnosis and stage of pregnancy.

Frequently asked questions

Does buttock pain always mean sciatica?

No. Pelvic girdle pain, haemorrhoids, contractions and other conditions can affect this broad area. Pain radiating down a leg with tingling or numbness makes a nerve cause more likely, but needs assessment.

Can pelvic girdle pain hurt my baby?

Confirmed pelvic girdle pain itself does not harm the baby. That reassurance does not apply to every unexplained pelvic pain, so new or severe symptoms still need checking.

Can I still have a vaginal birth?

Usually yes when the problem is pelvic girdle pain. Discuss comfortable positions and support with your maternity team; individual birth decisions depend on the whole pregnancy.

Should I keep my knees apart when turning in bed?

Keeping them comfortably together can help some people with pelvic girdle pain. Move within a comfortable range and ask a physiotherapist to demonstrate an approach that suits you.

Can the pain reveal whether I am having a boy or a girl?

No. The presence, side or severity of buttock or pelvic pain does not reliably indicate fetal sex.

Do waters always break in a gush?

No. A slow trickle can also be leaking amniotic fluid. Call your maternity service if you suspect it rather than waiting for more fluid.

Is bleeding from a pile always harmless?

No. New or persistent bleeding needs assessment. Heavy bleeding, large clots or feeling faint needs urgent help, even if you have had haemorrhoids before.

Is complete bed rest the best treatment?

Usually not. Suitable movement, rest breaks and targeted treatment are more useful. If pain prevents movement, ask for a review and an assessment of clot risk.

Should I avoid all pain medicine while pregnant?

No. Appropriate treatment matters. Ask about a pregnancy-suitable medicine and dose; do not substitute ibuprofen or a borrowed prescription without advice.

Will the pain definitely stop after delivery?

Not necessarily. Many people improve, but persistent pelvic pain or haemorrhoids may need ongoing treatment. New nerve, bladder or bowel symptoms remain urgent after birth.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
